text: Before the gray Gothic towers, before the gargoyles and the quiet courtyards, there was a different University of Chicago.
It opened in the 1850s, and it stood about two and a half miles north of where the campus sits today, near 35th Street and Cottage Grove Avenue.
The land came from Stephen A.
Douglas, the United States senator from Illinois.
Douglas first offered the tract to the Presbyterians, on the condition that they raise a hundred thousand dollars for a building.
So he gave the ten acres to a group of Baptists instead, and the school was chartered in 1857, with Douglas himself as the first president of its board of trustees.
That school never had enough money.
The financial panic of 1857 wiped out most of the early pledges almost as soon as it opened.
Douglas died in 1861, and his name was a problem for fundraisers.
He had written the Kansas-Nebraska Act, the law that let new territories vote slavery in, and many donors in the North wanted nothing to do with anything attached to him.
The trustees built anyway, past what they could afford.
They put up a five-story main building of stone and kept enrolling students even as the bills came due.
The debt climbed for thirty years.
In 1886 the creditors foreclosed, the classes stopped, and the first University of Chicago was finished.
It had run for nearly three decades and never escaped the hole it started in.
